title: FIFA Scraps World Cup Private Equity Plan After Global Revolt
excerpt: Gianni Infantino abandoned his $4.2 billion sell-off scheme within 72 hours of its leak, after UEFA threatened a full boycott and his own senior officials turned against him.
body:
• FIFA President Gianni Infantino scrapped plans to sell a 20% stake in a new $20 billion World Cup entity to private investors, including Joshua Kushner's Thrive Capital, after facing opposition from across world football.
  • UEFA and all 55 European member nations unanimously voted to boycott men's and women's World Cups, while CONCACAF and the AFC also rejected the proposal.
  • Infantino's own senior advisor Carlos Cordeiro resigned and FIFA COO Kevin Lamour publicly denounced the scheme as "the project of one person," raising questions about the FIFA president's future ahead of his 2027 re-election bid.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino on Friday abandoned his plan to sell part of the World Cup's commercial rights to private investors, backing down in the face of a unified global revolt that engulfed world football in barely three days. The proposal, which would have raised up to $4.2 billion by selling roughly 20% of a new entity called FIFA Forward Enterprise, collapsed after European, Asian, and North American federations lined up against it — and Infantino's own top officials broke ranks.

"Having listened carefully to all the views, it has become clear that the project has created divisions of a nature that, regardless of the level of support, are no longer in the interest of the objective set out in the first place," Infantino said in a statement. "This proposal will not proceed."

The Plan and the Backlash

The scheme, first leaked on Tuesday, July 28, envisioned the creation of FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) — a controlled subsidiary consolidating FIFA's commercial and event operations, valued at $20 billion. Joshua Kushner's Thrive Capital, whose brother Jared Kushner is the son-in-law of U.S. President Donald Trump, was positioned to lead the investor group. J.P. Morgan was advising on the deal.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=7DjyUbFMDSQ

FIFA had argued the minority stake sale would fund global sports development, with each of its 211 member associations receiving up to $40 million — a significant increase from the current $8 million per cycle. Infantino wrote directly to federations, setting a September 19 deadline for acceptance.

The response was swift and devastating. UEFA, representing European football's 55 member nations, held an emergency meeting on July 30 and voted unanimously to boycott all FIFA competitions, including the men's and women's World Cups.

"The soul and governance of football are not assets to trade — especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially. None of us are the owners of football. It is not FIFA's to sell."

— UEFA statement

CONCACAF, the North and Central American body, and the Asian Football Confederation both issued statements rejecting the proposal, though they stopped short of a boycott. Norway's football federation president Lise Klaveness called it "a very serious situation" and said the word "blackmail" had been used by fellow European delegates.

Internal Revolt

What made Friday's collapse inevitable was not just external opposition but the disintegration of Infantino's own inner circle. Carlos Cordeiro — a former Goldman Sachs banker, U.S. Soccer president, and key architect of the 2026 World Cup — resigned as Infantino's senior advisor.

"I cannot stand by while FIFA considers selling a stake in the World Cup," Cordeiro said. "I had no involvement in this proposal, and I oppose it unequivocally. It is a bad deal for FIFA's member associations, a bad deal for football, and a bad deal for the long-term future of the game."

Hours later, FIFA's own chief operating officer Kevin Lamour delivered the most damaging blow from within the organisation.

"It is the project of one person. Not only must this project not go ahead, but the time has now come for football political leaders to ask themselves the right questions and make the right decisions. And if that means I lose my job, then so be it."

— Kevin Lamour, FIFA Chief Operating Officer

Implications for Asian Football

The AFC's rejection of the proposal carries weight for football development across Asia, including India. FIFA's existing Forward Programme channels development funds to federations like the All India Football Federation, and the collapse of FFE means the promised $40 million windfall per member will not materialise. For emerging football nations relying on FIFA development grants, the episode raises questions about how future funding increases will be structured without private capital injection.

What's Next

While Infantino moved quickly to kill the proposal, the fallout may prove harder to contain. UEFA said Saturday that the FIFA president had "lost confidence" and issued a thinly veiled call for his resignation, describing the proposal as a "shabby, backroom, opaque deal."

Infantino, who had expected to sail toward a third full term in March 2027 with near-unanimous backing, now faces the most precarious moment of his decade-long tenure. According to the Wall Street Journal, he had recently anticipated support from at least 200 of FIFA's 211 member associations — a number that now looks optimistic.

"Moving forward, my intent is to bring all interested parties back together in the coming days and weeks in the spirit of shared interest in our game," Infantino said. But with UEFA already announcing plans to propose a new funding model through the existing FIFA Forward Programme, the balance of power in world football has shifted — and rebuilding trust will require far more than a single reversal.
